description: The 'Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)' is not attested in Paraguayan or Guaraní tradition. The Cheyenne are a North American Plains people (Montana, Oklahoma) with no historical presence in Paraguay. The closest Guaraní analogue is the Yaguareté-Abá (jaguar shapeshifter) or forest guardian spirits (Yvyraija) documented by Métraux.
source: Métraux, 'Ethnography of the Guaraní'; Cheyenne historical range (Great Plains, North America)
research_notes: Cheyenne are North American Plains people; record misattributes them to Paraguay. No Guaraní 'wildcat spirit' matching this description exists in ethnographic literature. Real analogue: Yaguareté-Abá (jaguar shapeshifter) or Yvyraija (forest owner spirits).

description: The 'Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)' is not attested in Chilean or Mapuche tradition. The Cheyenne are North American Plains people with no presence in Chile. Mapuche tradition features the Ngürü (fox spirit) and ngen (nature owners), but no wildcat spirit matching Cheyenne cosmology. The record appears fabricated.
source: Bacigalupo, 'Mapuche Religion'; Cheyenne historical range (Great Plains, North America)
research_notes: Cheyenne are North American; no presence in Chile. Mapuche have Ngürü (fox) and ngen nature spirits, not a Cheyenne-derived wildcat spirit. Fabricated entry.

description: The 'Wildcat Trickster of Quechua' is not independently attested in Quechua tradition. Andean mythology features the fox (atoc) as primary trickster and the puma as a powerful being, but no specific 'wildcat trickster.' The closest analogue is the Andean fox trickster cycle documented by Arguedas and Flores Ochoa.
source: Arguedas, 'Dioses y hombres de Huarochirí'; Flores Ochoa, 'Pastores de alpacas'; Quechua oral tradition
research_notes: No specific 'wildcat trickster' in Quechua sources. Fox (atoc) is the primary trickster; puma is a sacred animal. Record likely conflates fox trickster cycles with a generic wildcat label.

description: The 'Wolf Animal-Spirit of Muisca' is not attested in Muisca mythology. The Muisca (Altiplano Cundiboyacense, Colombia) had no wolves—wolves are absent from South America. Muisca deities include Bochica, Chía, Sué, Chibchacum, and Bachué; snip animal spirits include the snake and bear-fox Nencatacoa. The record appears fabricated.
source: Ocampo López, 'Mitos y leyendas indígenas de Colombia'; Muisca mythology (no wolves in South America)
research_notes: Wolves never existed in South America. Muisca animal spirits: snake (Meicuchuca's wife), bear-fox Nencatacoa, condor. 'Wolf' entry is a fabrication or misattribution of Northern Hemisphere motifs.

description: The 'Wolf Deity (Mapuche)' is not attested in Mapuche tradition. Wolves are absent from South America; snip the Mapuche have no wolf deity. Mapuche cosmology features Ngünechen, the ngen (nature owners), wekufe spirits, and animal spirits like the fox (Ngürü) and puma. The record misapplies Northern Hemisphere wolf motifs.
source: Bacigalupo, 'Mapuche Religion'; Latcham, 'La organización social y las creencias religiosas de los antiguos araucanos'; South American fauna (no wolves)
research_notes: Wolves absent from South America. Mapuche animal spirits: fox (Ngürü), puma, condor. 'Wolf deity' is a Northern Hemisphere motif misattributed to Mapuche.

description: The 'Wolf Guardian of Mapuche' is not attested in Mapuche tradition. Wolves never inhabited South America. Mapuche guardianship involves the ngen (place-owners) and machi (shamans) who mediate with spirits. The closest analogues are ngen-wenu (owner of the sky) or ngen-mapu (owner of the land), not a wolf figure.
source: Bacigalupo, 'Mapuche Religion'; South American fauna (no wolves)
research_notes: Wolves absent from South America. Mapuche has ngen (place spirits) and machi as spiritual guardians. Fabricated entry applying Eurasian wolf symbolism.

description: The 'Wolf Guardian of Muisca' is not attested in Muisca tradition. Wolves never existed in South America. Muisca guardianship is associated with Bochica (civilizer hero), the zipa/zaque rulers, and the sacred lakes (Guatavita, Iguaque). No wolf figures appear in Muisca mythology documented by Ocampo López.
source: Ocampo López, 'Mitos y leyendas indígenas de Colombia'; Muisca mythology; South American fauna (no wolves)
research_notes: Wolves absent from South America. Muisca guardians: Bochica, sacred lakes, rulers. Fabricated entry.

description: The 'Wolf Nature-Spirit (Tupi)' is not attested in Tupi-Guarani tradition. Wolves are absent from South America. Tupi-Guarani cosmology features the culture hero Mboi-Tatá (fire serpent), the trickster Curupira, and the jaguar (Yaguareté) as a powerful being. No wolf spirits exist in the ethnography of Métraux or Darcy Ribeiro.
source: Métraux, 'La religion des Tupinamba'; Darcy Ribeiro, 'O Povo Brasileiro'; Tupi-Guarani mythology; South American fauna (no wolves)
research_notes: Wolves absent from South America. Tupi-Guarani beings: Curupira, Mboi-Tatá, Yaguareté, Caipora. Wolf entry is fabricated.

description: The 'Wolf Nature-Spirit of Muisca' is not attested in Muisca tradition. Wolves never existed in South America. Muisca nature spirits are associated with lakes (Guatavita, Iguaque), mountains, and the rainbow (Cuchavira). Animal beings include the snake and bear-fox Nencatacoa. This entry misapplies Northern Hemisphere wolf symbolism.
source: Ocampo López, 'Mitos y leyendas indígenas de Colombia'; South American fauna (no wolves)
research_notes: Wolves absent from South America. Muisca water/earth spirits: lake guardians, Cuchavira (rainbow). Fabricated wolf entry.

description: The 'Wolf Trickster (Mapuche)' is not attested in Mapuche tradition. Wolves are absent from South America. Mapuche trickster figures include the wekufe (harmful spirits) and the kalku (sorcerer), but no wolf trickster. The fox (Ngürü) appears in some tales but not as a primary trickster. This is a fabricated entry applying Eurasian motifs.
source: Bacigalupo, 'Mapuche Religion'; South American fauna (no wolves)
research_notes: Wolves absent from South America. Mapuche has wekufe/kalku as harmful agents, fox (Ngürü) in minor roles. Fabricated.

description: The 'Bear Deity (Laotian)' is not attested in Colombian or Muisca tradition. The description describes a Laotian (Southeast Asian) moon bear deity tied to lunar cycles and rice agriculture—completely unrelated to Colombia. The Muisca had no bear deities; snip spectacled bears (ukumari) exist in the Andes but lack a moon-bear lunar deity in Muisca sources.
source: Laotian animism (moon bear); Muisca mythology (no bear deity); South American fauna (spectacled bear present but no lunar bear deity)
research_notes: Entry describes Laotian moon bear deity (Southeast Asia) but assigns to Colombia. Muisca: no bear deity. Spectacled bear (ukumari) exists but no lunar cult. Gross misattribution.

description: The Boto (Encantado) is the Amazon river dolphin shapeshifter of Brazilian Amazon folklore. At night it becomes a handsome man in white clothing with a hat hiding its blowhole, attends riverside festivals, seduces women, and returns to the river by dawn. Children from these unions are 'filhos do boto.
source: Cascudo, 'Geografia dos mitos brasileiros'; Barbosa Rodrigues, 'Poranduba Amazonense'; Brazilian Amazon oral tradition
research_notes: Well-documented Brazilian Amazon folklore. Verified across multiple ethnographic sources. Living tradition in Amazon communities.

description: The Tuatha Dé Danann ('People of the Goddess Danu') are the pre-Christian divine race of Irish mythology, arriving with four treasures. They defeated the Fir Bolg and Fomorians, then withdrew into sídhe mounds when the Milesians invaded. Key figures: the Dagda, Lugh, the Morrígan, Brigid, Nuada, Manannán mac Lir. Documented in Lebor Gabála Érenn and the Mythological Cycle.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Cath Maige Tuired; MacKillop, 'Dictionary of Celtic Mythology'; Irish Mythological Cycle
research_notes: Core Irish mythological race. Well-attested in medieval manuscripts (Lebor Gabála, Cath Maige Tuired). Expert-level documentation.

description: The Leannán Sídhe ('fairy lover') is a female fairy of the Aos Sí who takes a human lover, granting poetic inspiration but draining their life force so they die young. W. B. Yeats popularized her as a vampiric muse: 'The Gaelic poets die young, for she is restless.' Earlier sources (Lady Wilde, 1887) describe her as a fairy mistress who becomes a slave if refused.
source: Yeats, 'Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry'; Wilde, 'Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms and Superstitions of Ireland'; Ó Súileabháin, 'The Truth about Leannán Sidhe'
research_notes: Well-attested Irish fairy muse figure. Yeats's vampiric interpretation is literary; earlier folklore has reciprocal relationship. Expert documentation.

description: The Redcap (powrie) is a malevolent goblin of Anglo-Scottish Border folklore. He haunts ruined castles, wears iron boots and a red cap dyed in victims' blood, carries a pikestaff, and throws stones at travelers. Driven off by Scripture or a crucifix, vanishing in flames and leaving a large tooth. The most famous is Robin Redcap, familiar of William de Soulis of Hermitage Castle.
source: Henderson, 'Folklore of the Northern Counties'; Briggs, 'An Encyclopedia of Fairies'; Scott, 'Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border' (1802); Scottish Border ballads
research_notes: Well-documented Border goblin. Specific historical connection to William de Soulis. Expert sources (Henderson, Briggs, Scott).

description: Scottish fairy tradition encompasses the Seelie and Unseelie Courts, trooping fairies (Sídhe), and solitary spirits like the brownie, glaistig, and each-uisge. Not a single being but a class of nature spirits inhabiting knolls (sídhe), lochs, and glens.
source: Campbell, 'Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands'; Briggs, 'An Encyclopedia of Fairies'; School of Scottish Studies Archives; Scottish Gaelic oral tradition
research_notes: Record's current description erroneously describes Polish fairies (rusałka, boginka). Scottish fairy tradition is distinct and well-documented. Corrected to Scottish-specific beings.

description: The Skitters (Na Fir Chlis, 'the Nimble Men') are the fairy dancers of the Aurora Borealis in Scottish Gaelic tradition. Seen as multicolored lights or dancing warrior figures in the northern sky, their lively dancing foretells fair weather; snip wild, rapid movement is an ill omen. They are one of three hosts of fallen angels: fairies on land, Blue Men in the sea, and Nimble Men in the sky.
source: Campbell, 'Popular Tales of the West Highlands'; Mackenzie, 'Scottish Folk-Lore and Folk Life'; Gaelic oral tradition (Na Fir Chlis)
research_notes: Authentic Scottish Gaelic aurora tradition. 'Na Fir Chlis' = Nimble Men. Well-documented by Campbell. Expert source quality.

description: The Sluagh (Sluagh na Marbh, 'host of the dead') are the unforgiven dead in Irish and Scottish Gaelic folklore. They fly in a crescent host like birds, sweeping up souls of the dying—especially those who die unshriven—and carrying them westward over the sea. They cannot cross running water or enter a house with a lighted candle.
source: MacKillop, 'Dictionary of Celtic Mythology'; Spence, 'The Magic Arts in Celtic Britain'; Gaelic oral tradition (Irish & Scottish)
research_notes: Core Gaelic death-belief. Well-attested in both Irish and Scottish traditions. Expert documentation.

description: The Each-Uisge (Gaelic 'water horse') is the deadliest water horse of Scottish and Irish folklore, inhabiting sea lochs and freshwater lochs. It shape-shifts into a fine horse, pony, handsome man, or enormous bird (boobrie). If mounted, the rider's skin adheres and the each-uisge drags them to the deepest water, devouring the whole body except the liver.
source: Campbell, 'Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands'; Briggs, 'An Encyclopedia of Fairies'; MacPhail, 'Folklore from the Hebrides'; Gray, 'Legends of the Cairngorms'
research_notes: Well-documented Highland water horse. Distinct from kelpie (rivers). Multiple collected tales. Expert sources.

description: The Pwca (Púca, Pooka) is a Welsh shapeshifting spirit cognate with the Irish púca. It appears as a horse, goat, or human with animal features, leading travelers on wild rides but doing no lasting harm. Controlled by sharp spurs (cold iron). Associated with Samhain; snip 1 November is 'Pwca's Day.' Regional forms include a goblin in Glamorgan, an eagle in Pembroke, a black goat in Radnor.
source: Sikes, 'British Goblins'; Rhys, 'Celtic Folklore'; Welsh Folk Museum archives; Lady Wilde, 'Ancient Legends'
research_notes: Well-documented Welsh cognate of Irish púca. Regional variants recorded. Expert documentation.

description: The Púca is an Irish shapeshifting spirit (púca, plural púcaí) of Celtic, English, and Channel Islands folklore. It appears as a sleek black horse with golden eyes, or as goat, cat, rabbit, raven, fox, wolf, goblin, or dog—always dark-furred. It entices riders on wild nocturnal journeys but unlike the kelpie does not drown them. Controlled by sharp spurs (cold iron).
source: Croker, 'Fairy Legends'; Keightley, 'Fairy Mythology'; Wilde, 'Ancient Legends'; Yeats, 'Fairy and Folk Tales'; Breatnach, 'The Púca'; MacKillop, 'Dictionary of Celtic Mythology'
research_notes: Core Irish shapeshifter. Extensive documentation across oral and literary sources. Expert quality.

description: The Púca (or Pook-al) is a regional Irish name for the púca, emphasizing its horse form: a shiny black steed that lures riders, or a goat with long horns, or a dark-haired slightly deformed human. It tangles hair, spits in drinks, steals items, but can also guide travelers. Must be kept fed or it turns angry. Samhain is 'Púca Night.' The name 'Pook-al' reflects the Anglo-Irish pronunciation.
source: Croker, 'Fairy Legends'; Keightley, 'Fairy Mythology'; Wilde, 'Ancient Legends'; MacKillop, 'Dictionary of Celtic Mythology'
research_notes: Variant name for the same Irish púca. Same attestation as p-ca entry. Expert documentation.

description: The Crogall is a Scottish water beast of Highland lochs and rivers, resembling a kelpie but more animalistic and brutal. It appears as a dark, shaggy water horse or massive hound with seaweed-tangled mane, glowing marsh-fire eyes, reversed hooves, and jagged shell-like teeth. In human form: a soaked, wild-eyed man with water plants in his hair.
source: Campbell, 'Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands'; Mackenzie, 'Scottish Folk-Lore and Folk Life'; Highland oral tradition
research_notes: Distinct from kelpie and each-uisge. Campbell records it as less intelligent, more brute-force. Expert Highland sources.

description: The Cyhyraeth is a Welsh death-omen spirit, primarily a disembodied moaning voice heard three times (growing fainter each time) before a death, especially during epidemics or disasters. Associated with the River Tywi in Dyfed and the Glamorganshire coast (where it warns of shipwrecks with corpse-lights).
source: Owen, 'Welsh Folk-Lore'; Sikes, 'British Goblins'; Peregrine Netzine; Welsh oral tradition
research_notes: Well-attested Welsh death portent. Distinct from Gwrach-y-Rhibyn but sometimes conflated. Good documentation.

description: The Cóiste Bodhar (Irish 'deaf coach') is the death coach of Irish folklore: a black, windowless carriage pulled by three headless black horses, driven by the Dullahan (headless horseman carrying his rotting head). It collects souls of the wicked and those with unsettled debts, calling the dying person's name at crossroads—death follows within three days.
source: MacKillop, 'Dictionary of Celtic Mythology'; Irish oral tradition; Yeats, 'Fairy and Folk Tales'
research_notes: Core Irish death-omen. Dullahan as driver is standard. Well-documented in MacKillop and folklore collections.

description: The Cù Sídhe (Scottish Gaelic 'fairy hound') is a massive spectral hound the size of a Highland calf, with shaggy dark green or ghostly white fur, large rounded ears glowing blood-red, emerald eyes, and dinner-plate paws leaving no tracks. It wanders the Highlands and moors on misty nights, howling three times to foretell a death.
source: Campbell, 'Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands'; Briggs, 'An Encyclopedia of Fairies'; MacKillop, 'Dictionary of Celtic Mythology'; Scottish Gaelic oral tradition
research_notes: Distinct from Welsh Cŵn Annwn (solitary vs pack). Three howls = death omen. Expert Highland sources.

description: The Cŵn Annwn ('Hounds of Annwn') are spectral hounds of the Welsh Otherworld (Annwn), white or coal-black with glowing red/green eyes and distinctive red ears. They hunt in packs led by Arawn (king of Annwn) or later Gwyn ap Nudd, chasing souls of the wicked and unshriven, especially at Samhain. Their baying grows louder as they approach.
source: First Branch of the Mabinogi (Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed); Fourth Branch (Math fab Mathonwy); 'Culhwch and Olwen'; MacKillop, 'Dictionary of Celtic Mythology'
research_notes: Core Welsh Otherworld hounds. Mabinogi attestation (Arawn). Red ears = Otherworld mark. Expert medieval Welsh sources.

description: Wee Willie Winkie is a Scottish nursery rhyme character created by poet William Miller in 1841 ('Whistle-Binkie: Stories for the Fireside'), not a folkloric fairy. The rhyme personifies sleep: 'Wee Willie Winkie rins through the toon... Tirlin' at the window... Are the weans in their bed, for it's now ten o'clock?' It became a bedtime entity alongside the Sandman and Scandinavian Ole Lukøje.
source: Miller, 'Whistle-Binkie' (1841); Opie, 'Oxford Dictionary of Nursery Rhymes'; Scottish literary history
research_notes: Literary creation (1841), not folklore. Personification of sleep. Record misclassifies as 'fairy'/'demonic-entity'. Corrected to literary nursery rhyme origin.

description: The Tupilaq (tupilait pl.) is an Inuit (Greenland) avenging monster fabricated by an angakkuq (shaman) from animal parts (bone, skin, hair, sinew) and sometimes human remains, given life by ritual chants. Sent into the sea to destroy a specific enemy. Risky: if the target has greater magical power, the tupilaq rebounds to kill its maker—only public confession neutralizes it.
source: Rasmussen, 'Across Arctic America'; Kleivan & Sonne, 'Eskimos: Greenland and Canada'; Ehrlich, 'This Cold Heaven'; Inuit oral tradition (Greenland, Canada)
research_notes: Well-documented Inuit shamanic construct. Regional variants recorded. Expert ethnographic sources (Rasmussen, Kleivan & Sonne).

description: The Qalupalik (Qallupilluit) is an Inuit sea creature of Greenland and Arctic Canada that kidnaps children wandering too close to ice floes. Described as green-skinned, slimy, with long hair, webbed hands, scales, fins, wearing an amauti (woman's parka) made of eider feathers to carry victims. Emits a paralyzing shrill sound; snip can shape-shift (pilutitaminik).
source: Boas, 'Qallupilluit' (InuitMyths.com); Christopher, 'The Qallupilluit Strange Beings from the Sea Depths'; Routledge, 'Do You See Ice?'; Inuit oral tradition (Nunavut, Greenland, Alaska)
research_notes: Well-attested Inuit child-snatcher figure. Still living tradition in Greenland. Good documentation.

description: The Troll is a pervasive anthropomorphic being of Scandinavian folklore, ranging from massive ogrish giants (30–100+ feet, hairy, tusks, flat nose, stone-grey) to smaller mound-dwelling beings (human-sized, comely, garments of moss). Nocturnal—sunlight turns them to stone; snip church bells and crosses drive them away. Live in mountains, deep forests, caves in small family units.
source: Asbjørnsen & Moe, 'Norske Folkeeventyr'; Lindow, 'Trolls: An Unnatural History'; Scandinavian oral tradition; laestadian records
research_notes: Core Nordic being. Two distinct traditions (giant vs small). Well-documented across Scandinavia. Good source quality.

description: The Kelpie is a shape-shifting water spirit of Scottish and Irish folklore, inhabiting rivers, streams, and lochs. Typically appears as a magnificent horse with dripping mane, or a handsome man. Predatory: lures travelers to mount, then skin becomes adhesive and it drags them underwater to drown and devour (except liver). Can be controlled by an iron bridle or learning its true name.
source: Briggs, 'An Encyclopedia of Fairies'; Campbell, 'Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands'; Scottish & Irish oral tradition
research_notes: Core Celtic water horse. River-dwelling (vs each-uisge in sea/lochs). Iron bridle control. Expert documentation.

description: The Redcap (Robin Redcap) is a murderous goblin of English Border folklore (Northumbria), haunting ruined castles—especially those of tyrannical lords. Wears a red cap soaked in victims' blood, iron boots, carries an iron pikestaff, throws huge stones. Repelled by religious symbols. Famous as familiar of Lord Soulis of Hermitage Castle (ballad 'Lord Soulis' in Scott's 'Minstrelsy').
source: Henderson, 'Folklore of the Northern Counties'; Briggs, 'An Encyclopedia of Fairies'; Scott, 'Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border'; Northumbrian oral tradition
research_notes: Same entity as Scottish Redcap, English Border variant. Lord Soulis connection. Expert sources.

description: English fairy tradition encompasses diverse beings: the trooping fairies of hills and mounds, solitary spirits like the brownie (household helper), boggart (malevolent house spirit), pixie (Southwest), and the Lincolnshire/Fenland Tiddy Mun. Not a single entity but a class.
source: Briggs, 'An Encyclopedia of Fairies'; Tongue, 'Forgotten Folk-Tales'; Evans-Wentz, 'The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries'; English Folklore Society collections
research_notes: Record's current description erroneously describes Polish fairies (rusałka, boginka). English fairy tradition is distinct. Corrected to English-specific beings.

description: The Nisse (Tomte, Tomtenisse, Tonttu) is a Nordic household spirit: small, human-like, gray-clad with a red pointed cap, dwelling in farmstead barns, stables, or under floorboards. Performs chores (threshing, animal care, carpentry) in exchange for a bowl of porridge (rømmegrøt or rice pudding) with butter on Christmas Eve.
source: Asbjørnsen & Moe, 'Norske Folkeeventyr'; Faye, 'Norske Folkesagn'; Afzelius; Christiansen; Feilberg; Olaus Magnus, 'Historia de Gentibus Septentrionalibus' (1555)
research_notes: Core Nordic household spirit. Porridge offering central. Clothing gift = departure motif (ML 7015). Expert documentation.
